lessons.title: Preparing Colonies for Winter
lessons.body:
In many African regions, winter is not a deep freeze but a cool, dry season with little to no nectar flow. Bees still need preparation. Start by assessing each colony's strength 6-8 weeks before the cool season. A strong colony has at least 8 frames covered with bees and a laying queen. Weak colonies (fewer than 5 frames) should be combined with a stronger hive using the newspaper method: place a sheet of newspaper between two brood boxes, make a few slits, and stack the weak colony on top of the strong one. The bees will chew through and merge peacefully.

Reduce the entrance to about 2-3 cm using a wooden cleat or grass bundle. This helps the bees defend against robbers and keeps out cold drafts. Remove any empty supers and unused frames to reduce the space the bees must heat. In areas with cold nights, consider moving hives to a spot that gets morning sun and is sheltered from wind. If you use top bar hives, close the ends with a follower board and insulate the roof with dry grass or a sack.

Ensure the hive has adequate honey stores: a strong colony needs 15-20 kg of honey to survive a 3-4 month dearth. If stores are low, feed thick sugar syrup (2 parts sugar to 1 part water) in a feeder placed inside the hive to prevent robbing. Stop feeding when the bees stop taking it or when brood rearing slows. Also, treat for varroa mites before winterâuse approved strips or oxalic acid dribbling according to local guidelines. A healthy colony with low mite load survives better.

Finally, tilt the hive slightly forward so condensation runs out, and ensure the roof is watertight. In African savannahs, termites can be a problem; place hive stands in oil cans or use ash around the legs. With these steps, your colonies will be ready for the cool season.

lessons.title: Winter Hive Insulation and Ventilation
lessons.body:
In African winters, temperatures may drop to 5-10Â°C at night, especially in highlands. Bees cluster to stay warm, but they also need ventilation to avoid moisture buildup. Insulation helps them conserve energy. Use locally available materials: dry banana leaves, grass, or old blankets. Wrap the hive body with a layer, leaving the entrance clear. For Langstroth hives, place a quilt box on top: a shallow box filled with wood shavings or dry rice husks, covered with a breathable cloth. This absorbs moisture and adds insulation. In top bar hives, stuff dry grass between the follower board and the end wall.

Ventilation is critical. Without it, warm moist air from the cluster condenses on cold surfaces, dripping on bees and causing chill or disease. Drill a 2-3 cm hole near the top of the hive body (above the brood nest) and cover it with wire mesh to prevent robbers. In Langstroth hives, you can also prop the outer cover up slightly with a twig to allow air exchange. But avoid strong drafts directly on the cluster. The entrance should remain open but reduced to 2-3 cm. If you use a screened bottom board, keep it open for ventilation; in very cold areas, you may close it partially.

Monitor humidity inside the hive. If you see mold or wetness on inner covers, increase ventilation. A simple hygrometer can help, but visual checks suffice. On sunny days, bees may take cleansing flights; ensure the entrance is not blocked by dead bees or debris. Remove any snow or frost from the entrance. In areas with cold winds, place a windbreak of grass or sticks on the windward side. Remember, bees generate heat by eating honey and shivering; proper insulation and ventilation reduce honey consumption and stress. This means more bees survive to spring buildup.

lessons.title: Winter Feeding and Moisture Control
lessons.body:
Winter feeding is often necessary when honey stores are below 10 kg. Use thick sugar syrup (2:1 sugar to water by volume) or fondant. Syrup can ferment or freeze in cold weather, so fondant is safer. To make fondant, mix 4 kg sugar with 1 liter water and 1 teaspoon cream of tartar; heat gently until dissolved, then cool and knead into a stiff dough. Place it on top of the frames, over the cluster, so bees can reach it. For syrup, use an inside feeder (like a division board feeder) to prevent robbing. Never feed outside the hive in winter.

Moisture control is as important as feeding. Bees produce water vapor from respiration and from consuming honey. If this moisture condenses and drips, bees can chill and die. Use a quilt box or moisture-absorbing material like dry newspaper or burlap on top of the frames. Replace it when damp. Ensure the hive has a slight forward tilt so condensation runs down and out the entrance. In humid regions, increase ventilation by opening the top hole more. Avoid sealing the hive completely; air must circulate.

Check stores every 2-3 weeks on warm days (above 10Â°C). Lift the hive from the back; if it feels light, add fondant. Do not open the hive fully in cold weather; just lift the cover enough to add feed. If you see dead bees at the entrance, clear them. Also, ensure the entrance is not blocked by ice or snow. In some African areas, winter is dry, so provide a water source nearby if bees are active. But avoid open water that can drown bees; use a shallow dish with stones. With proper feeding and moisture management, your colonies will emerge strong in spring.

lessons.title: Spring Buildup and Swarm Prevention
lessons.body:
Spring signals the start of nectar flow and rapid brood rearing. As soon as you see bees bringing in pollen and the queen increasing laying, it's time for management. First, inspect the hive on a warm day (above 15Â°C). Check for the queen, brood pattern, and stores. If the colony survived winter but is weak (fewer than 4 frames of bees), consider combining it with another weak colony or giving it a frame of capped brood from a strong hive. This boosts numbers.

Swarm prevention is crucial in spring. Swarming happens when the hive becomes crowded and the queen has nowhere to lay. To prevent it, provide space early. Add a super or an empty box with frames when the brood nest has 7-8 frames of bees. If using a top bar hive, add empty bars at the back. Also, remove any queen cells you find during inspectionsâbut only if you can do it every 7-10 days. Alternatively, make a split: remove 2-3 frames of brood with bees and a queen cell to a new hive, and give the original hive new frames to draw. This mimics swarming but keeps your apiary growing.

Ensure the queen has room to lay. If she is old (over 2 years) and brood pattern is spotty, replace her with a new mated queen. In African beekeeping, local queens are often available from other beekeepers. Also, watch for signs of disease like chalkbrood or foulbrood. If you see mummified larvae, remove and burn the frames. Feed 1:1 sugar syrup to stimulate brood rearing if nectar flow is slow. But stop feeding once honey supers are on to avoid contaminating honey. With these steps, your colonies will build up strong and be ready for the main flow.

lessons.title: Summer Management for Honey Flow
lessons.body:
Summer is the main honey flow in many African regions, especially after rains. Your goal is to maximize honey production while keeping colonies healthy. Before the flow, ensure each hive has a laying queen and at least 10 frames of bees. Add honey supers (for Langstroth) or extra bars (for top bar) when the first nectar appears. Use a queen excluder if you want honey without brood, but in Africa, many beekeepers skip it to allow the queen to move up; just harvest only capped honey frames. Inspect every 7-10 days to check for swarm cells and to add more space as needed.

During the flow, avoid frequent full inspections; it disturbs bees and may reduce yield. Instead, do quick checks from the back: lift the lid, look at the top bars, and see if bees are working. If the super is 80% full, add another. Harvest honey only when frames are at least 80% capped. Use a bee brush or gentle smoke to remove bees. Never harvest uncapped honey; it will ferment. Leave at least 10 kg of honey for the bees, especially if a dearth follows. In hot climates, ensure hives are shaded during the hottest part of the day; place them under trees or use a shade cloth. Provide water nearby.

Monitor for pests: ants, wax moths, and small hive beetles. Keep hives off the ground and use ant barriers like grease or ash. If you see wax moth larvae, remove affected frames and freeze them for 24 hours. For small hive beetles, use traps or diatomaceous earth. Also, watch for signs of American foulbrood: sunken, perforated cappings. If found, burn the hive and equipment. After the flow, when nectar slows, remove honey supers and store them dry to prevent moths. Reduce entrances to prevent robbing. With good summer management, you can harvest 20-30 kg per hive in a good year.

lessons.title: Fall Preparations and Disease Check
lessons.body:
Fall (autumn) is the time to prepare colonies for winter and to do a thorough disease check. In many African regions, fall is the end of the rainy season and the start of a dearth. After harvesting honey, inspect each hive carefully. Look for signs of disease: American foulbrood (sunken, dark cappings with a ropy mass), European foulbrood (twisted larvae), chalkbrood (white or black mummies), and nosema (dysentery). If you suspect foulbrood, isolate the hive and consult an extension officer. For chalkbrood, improve ventilation and replace the queen. For nosema, ensure good ventilation and feed clean syrup.

Check varroa mite levels using a sugar roll or alcohol wash. If you find more than 3 mites per 100 bees, treat with approved methods: oxalic acid dribbling (in broodless periods) or formic acid pads. In Africa, many beekeepers use traditional methods like tobacco smoke, but these are not effective. Use only approved treatments. Also, check for tracheal mites if bees have K-winged wings. Treat with menthol crystals if available.

Assess honey stores. A colony needs 15-20 kg to survive winter. If stores are low, feed thick syrup (2:1) until they stop taking it. Combine weak colonies with strong ones. Reduce entrances to 2-3 cm and add insulation. Remove any empty supers and store them properly to prevent wax moths. Clean the bottom board of debris. Finally, ensure the hive is watertight and tilted forward. In areas with cold winters, wrap the hive with insulation. With these fall preparations, your bees will be healthy and ready for the next season.

quiz.q: What is the recommended minimum number of frames covered with bees for a colony to be considered strong for winter?
quiz.explanation: A strong colony should have at least 8 frames covered with bees to survive winter.

quiz.q: Which method is used to combine a weak colony with a strong one?
quiz.explanation: The newspaper method involves placing newspaper between boxes so bees gradually merge.

quiz.q: How much honey does a strong colony need to survive a 3-4 month dearth?
quiz.explanation: A strong colony requires 15-20 kg of honey to survive a 3-4 month dearth.

quiz.q: What is the correct ratio for thick sugar syrup for winter feeding?
quiz.explanation: Thick syrup for winter is made with 2 parts sugar to 1 part water.

quiz.q: Why should you reduce the hive entrance in winter?
options: A) To keep out robbers and cold drafts
D) To allow queen to lay more eggs
quiz.explanation: A smaller entrance helps bees defend against robbers and reduces cold drafts.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a quilt box in winter?
options: A) To provide extra honey storage
B) To absorb moisture and insulate
quiz.explanation: A quilt box filled with absorbent material absorbs moisture and adds insulation.

quiz.q: How large should a top ventilation hole be?
quiz.explanation: A 2-3 cm hole covered with wire mesh provides adequate ventilation.

quiz.q: What is a sign of excess moisture in the hive?
options: B) Mold or wetness on inner cover
quiz.explanation: Mold or wetness on the inner cover indicates high humidity and poor ventilation.

quiz.q: Why is fondant preferred over syrup in cold weather?
options: B) It does not freeze or ferment
C) It is easier to make
quiz.explanation: Fondant does not freeze or ferment, making it safer for cold weather feeding.

quiz.q: How often should you check stores in winter?
quiz.explanation: Check stores every 2-3 weeks on warm days to ensure bees have enough food.

quiz.q: What is a sign that spring buildup has started?
quiz.explanation: Bees bringing in pollen indicates the colony is rearing brood and building up.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of swarming?
options: B) Crowded hive and no space for queen to lay
quiz.explanation: Swarming is triggered by overcrowding and lack of space for the queen to lay.

quiz.q: How can you prevent swarming?
quiz.explanation: Adding supers early provides space and reduces crowding, preventing swarming.

quiz.q: What is a split in beekeeping?
options: A) Dividing a colony into two
quiz.explanation: A split involves dividing a colony to create a new one, often to prevent swarming.

quiz.q: When should you add honey supers during summer?
quiz.explanation: Add supers when the first nectar appears to give bees space to store honey.

quiz.q: What percentage of capped honey should a frame have before harvesting?
quiz.explanation: Harvest only frames that are at least 80% capped to ensure honey is ripe.

quiz.q: How much honey should you leave for the bees after harvest?
quiz.explanation: Leave at least 10 kg of honey for the bees, especially if a dearth follows.

quiz.q: What is a common pest of honey bees in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Varroa mites, wax moths, and small hive beetles are all common pests in Africa.

quiz.q: How can you control wax moths?
quiz.explanation: Freezing affected frames for 24 hours kills wax moth larvae and eggs.

quiz.q: What is a sign of American foulbrood?
quiz.explanation: American foulbrood causes sunken, perforated cappings and a ropy mass.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect foulbrood?
quiz.explanation: Foulbrood is highly contagious; burning the hive and equipment is often necessary.

quiz.q: How many mites per 100 bees indicate a need for treatment?
quiz.explanation: More than 3 mites per 100 bees warrants treatment for varroa.

quiz.q: Which treatment is effective for varroa in broodless periods?
quiz.explanation: Oxalic acid dribbling is effective when no brood is present.

quiz.q: What is nosema?
quiz.explanation: Nosema is a fungal disease that causes dysentery in bees.

quiz.q: How can you prevent nosema?
quiz.explanation: Good ventilation helps prevent nosema by reducing moisture and stress.

quiz.q: What is the best time to treat for varroa?
quiz.explanation: Treat for varroa before winter to ensure healthy bees survive the cold.

quiz.q: What should you do with empty supers after harvest?
options: A) Leave them on the hive
quiz.explanation: Store empty supers dry to prevent wax moths and fermentation.

quiz.q: Why is it important to tilt the hive forward?
options: A) To let condensation run out
quiz.explanation: A slight forward tilt allows condensation to drain out, preventing moisture buildup.

quiz.q: What is a windbreak used for?
quiz.explanation: A windbreak protects hives from cold winds, reducing stress on bees.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of fall preparations?
quiz.explanation: Fall preparations focus on getting colonies healthy and strong for winter.
